name: White Oak Point band agreement under the Nelson Act (Mississippi Chippewa, White Oak band), signed September 6, 1889
aka: Nelson Act cession, White Oak Point band of Mississippi Chippewa
citation: Act of January 14, 1889, ch. 24, 25 Stat. 642; agreement printed in H. R. Ex. Doc. 247, 51st Cong., 1st sess.
nations: White Oak Point band of Mississippi Ojibwe (today within the Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe)
promises: Royce records that the White Oak band ceded its rights in the White Earth Reservation not needed for allotments, in the lands reserved by Article 1 of the 1867 treaty with the Chippewa of the Mississippi and their executive addition, and in the Red Lake Reservation not needed for allotments.

Section 1: the cession valid only if assented to in writing by two-thirds of the male adults over eighteen of the band; an Indian already holding an allotment not to be deprived of it or disturbed without his own separate consent.
Section 3: allotments in severalty; an Indian could take his allotment on the reservation where he lived instead of removing to White Earth.
Sections 4 and 5: pine lands examined, appraised and sold at public auction for no less than the appraised value.
Section 6: agricultural land not allotted sold to actual settlers under the homestead law at $1.25 an acre.
Section 7: net proceeds held in the Treasury as a permanent fund for all the Chippewa in Minnesota, drawing 5 percent interest paid yearly for fifty years, then divided among them.

breaches.what: The Minnesota Chippewa Tribe claimed in Indian Claims Commission Dockets 19 and 188 that Nelson Act land and timber proceeds were misspent and that land and timber were sold for less than full value. The claims were settled for $20 million, which the Court of Federal Claims awarded in May 1999.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Minnesota Chippewa Tribe v. United States, Dockets 19 and 188 (settlement), as described in the Bureau of Indian Affairs' testimony to the House Subcommittee on Indian and Alaska Native Affairs, March 1, 2012

source.title: Testimony of Mike Black, Director, Bureau of Indian Affairs, on H.R. 1272, Minnesota Chippewa Tribe Judgment Fund Distribution Act (March 1, 2012)

landTaken: Royce records the cession of the band's interest in the White Earth surplus, the 1867 Article 1 lands with their executive addition, and the Red Lake surplus. No acreage was taken from a primary source.
compensation: Net sale proceeds were to go into the Chippewa permanent fund (Section 7). The 1999 settlement of $20 million covers all six member bands of the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe.
today: In Chippewa Indians of Minnesota v. United States, 307 U.S. 1 (1939), the Supreme Court held that the 1889 Act and the cessions under it did not create a technical trust and did not bind Congress to the plan, so spending from the fund for the Indians' benefit was not a diversion; that ruling went against the Chippewa and is not counted as a breach. The Bureau of Indian Affairs testified in 2012 that no funds remained to divide in equal shares after the fifty years, and that the 1999 settlement money had been held in trust since June 22, 1999.

plain.promised: Allotments where people lived, no existing allotment taken without consent, and all land and timber sale money held in a fund for all Minnesota Chippewa at 5 percent interest for fifty years, then divided among them.
plain.happened: The Minnesota Chippewa Tribe claimed the sale money was misspent and land and timber sold below full value. Leech Lake, a member band, says the Act violated existing treaties. No formal finding has been located.
plain.today: The claims were settled for $20 million in 1999 for all six member bands. In 1939 the Supreme Court ruled against the Chippewa on spending from the fund. In 2012 the Bureau of Indian Affairs said no fund was left to divide.

nationVoice.summary: Chairman Arthur LaRose told the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs that the Nelson Act sought to open the bands' reservations to settlers and logging companies in clear violation of existing treaties, and that the Band now holds about 4 percent of its reservation.

openQuestions: The 1999 settlement is a compromise and is recorded as litigation, not a finding. No court or Commission finding specific to this cession was found.

That the White Oak Point band is today part of the Leech Lake Band is the researcher's understanding and is not stated in a source opened in this pass; the LaRose testimony speaks for Leech Lake generally.
Royce gives the date of the executive addition to the 1867 Article 1 lands as October 19, 1873 here and October 29, 1873 in the White Earth entry; not resolved.
Royce places this White Oak band cession under area 710 together with the Pillager agreement of August 21, 1889; treaties.json gives both entries the same scheduleTribes.
The agreement itself (H. R. Ex. Doc. 247) was not opened.
